titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The Battle of Tévar (tiradas 56–59, lines 960–1023)

sentences.t:
El conde es muy follón e dixo una vanidat:
“Grandes tuertos me tiene mio Çid el de Bivar.
sentences.l:
The count is very puffed-up and said a vanity:
“Great wrongs to-me has my Çid he of Bivar.
sentences.i: The count is a very arrogant man, and he spoke an empty boast: “Great are the wrongs my Çid of Vivar has done me.
sentences.n: Tirada 56 (assonance á) — the Çid tries in vain to calm the count (Pidal: El Cid trata en vano de calmar al conde). The line-ends are a single stressed á (vanidat, Bivar, grand, más, están, demandar, van, pinar, val, verdad …); grandes (968) and mensaje (975) end in á-e, the unstressed final e not counting. follón: an abusive word for an overbearing, worthless man; here it plainly means 'arrogant, puffed-up', paired with vanidat, 'a vain thing, an empty boast' (Pidal gives no footnote; the exact shade of follón is uncertain). dixo = dijo. tuertos, 'wrongs, injuries' (Latin tortum, 'twisted'); me tiene, 'has (done) to me', tener with the wrongs as its object. el de Bivar, 'he of Vivar'.

sentences.t:
Dentro en mi cort tuerto me tovo grand:
firióm el sobrino e non lo enmendó más;
sentences.l:
Within in my court wrong to-me he-did great:
struck-me the nephew and not it he-amended more;
sentences.i: In my own court he did me a great wrong: his nephew struck me, and he never made amends for it;
sentences.n: Dentro en mi cort, 'within my court'. Pidal's note to v. 962: the Çid, newly exiled, did in fact stay in Barcelona (his introduction, p. 18, n. 1). tovo = tuvo, old preterite of tener. firióm = me firió, 'struck me' (ferir = herir, f- for h-), the pronoun glued on after the verb. el sobrino, 'the nephew', i.e. the Çid's: the text does not name him and Pidal gives no note. enmendó, 'made amends'; non … más, 'never afterwards'.

sentences.t: agora córrem las tierras que en mi enpara están;
sentences.l: now raids-me the lands that in my protection are;
sentences.i: now he is raiding the lands that stand under my protection;
sentences.n: córrem = me corre, 'raids on me', with me as the dative of the person harmed; correr las tierras, 'to raid the lands'. enpara = amparo, 'protection'. Pidal's note to v. 958 points to this line: these were not the count's own lands but lands under his protectorate.

sentences.t:
non lo desafié nil torné [el] [a]mi[z]tad,
mas quando él me lo busca, ir gelo he yo demandar.”
sentences.l:
not him I-defied nor-to-him I-returned the friendship,
but since he from-me it seeks, go it-of-him will I demand.”
sentences.i: I never defied him nor renounced my friendship with him; but since he comes seeking it of me, I shall go and demand redress of him.”
sentences.n: desafié, 'I defied', the formal declaration of enmity. nil = ni le, 'nor to him'. [el] [a]mi[z]tad: the article el, the a and the z are all Pidal's restorations (italics in his print); el before a feminine noun in a- is the old usage (el amistad). Pidal's note to v. 965: tornar amistad was to withdraw the friendship presumed to exist among all noblemen, and the formula was 'tórnovos amistad et desafíovos por tal tuerto que ficistes a mí' ('I withdraw my friendship from you and defy you for such a wrong as you did me'). The count's point is that he had kept the forms and the Çid had not. quando, 'since' (causal). ir gelo he … demandar = se lo iré a demandar, 'I will go to demand it of him': a split future, the infinitive ir, then the pronouns gelo (= se lo, 'it of him'), then he; the lo is the satisfaction owed.

sentences.t:
Grandes son los poderes e a priessa llegando[s] van,
entre moros e cristianos gentes se le allegan grandes
adeliñan tras mio Çid el bueno de Bivar,
sentences.l:
Great are the forces and in haste gathering-themselves they-go,
between Moors and Christians hosts themselves to-him join great
they-make-straight after my Çid the good one of Bivar,
sentences.i: Great are his forces, and in haste they gather; Moors and Christians alike, great hosts rally to him; they make straight after my Çid, the good man of Vivar;
sentences.n: poderes, 'forces, troops'. a priessa, 'in haste'. llegando[s] van = se van llegando, 'they go gathering': llegarse, 'to come together', with the se glued on as -s; Pidal restores the s. entre moros e cristianos, 'Moors and Christians both' (entre … e). se le allegan, 'join themselves to him', the count. No punctuation stands at the end of v. 968 in Pidal's print; kept. adeliñan, 'they make straight for' (adeliñar, 'to head directly'). el bueno de Bivar, 'the good man of Vivar'.

sentences.i: three days and two nights they marched on, and overtook my Çid in the pine-wood of Tévar; they come on in such confidence that they mean to take him with their bare hands.
sentences.n: penssaron de andar, 'they set about marching' (pensar de + infinitive). alcançaron, 'overtook'. Tévar e el pinar: Pidal's note to v. 971 — it amounts to el pinar de Tévar, 'the pine-wood of Tévar', as at vv. 912 and 999; according to a document of 1209 the pine-wood lay at the confluence of the rivers Monroy and Tastavins, on the boundary of the provinces of Tarragona and Castellón. viene[n] esforçado[s] … cuyda[n]: Pidal restores the n, the s and the n, making the three forms plural (the count's men); esforçados, 'emboldened, confident'. cuydar, 'to think, expect'. a manos, 'with their hands'; se le … tomar, 'to take him', le the Çid, se the subjects' own interest; how se is construed here is not certain.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid don Rodrigo trae ganançia grand,
diçe de una sierra e llegava a un val.
sentences.l:
My Çid don Rodrigo brings booty great,
descends from a range and was-arriving at a valley.
sentences.i: My Çid don Rodrigo is carrying great booty; he comes down from a range of hills and was reaching a valley.
sentences.n: ganançia, 'gain, booty'. diçe: Pidal's note to v. 974, 'desciende', 'comes down' (deçir, 'to descend', not dezir, 'to say'). The present diçe beside the imperfect llegava is the poem's tense-mixing. sierra, 'mountain range'; val, 'valley'.

sentences.t:
Del conde don Remont venido lês mensaje;
mio Çid quando lo oyó, enbió pora allá:
sentences.l:
From-the count don Remont come to-them-is message;
my Çid when it he-heard, sent toward there:
sentences.i: From Count Remont a message has reached them; when my Çid heard it, he sent word back:
sentences.n: lês: so printed by Pidal, with a circumflex (like lâ at v. 914). It is read here as les + es, 'to them is', the circumflex marking two e's run together: venido lês mensaje = les es venido (un) mensaje, 'a message has come to them', ser as the auxiliary of a verb of motion. Pidal gives no footnote, so this analysis is uncertain. don Remont: Remont Verenguel (v. 998), the count of Barcelona, Ramón Berenguer. enbió = envió; pora allá, 'over there', i.e. to the count; the object (a messenger, word) is left unsaid.

sentences.t:
“digades al conde non lo tenga a mal,
de lo so non lievo nada, déxem ir en paz.”
sentences.l:
“may-you-tell to-the count not it he-hold for bad,
of the his not I-carry nothing, let-me go in peace.”
sentences.i: “Tell the count not to take it amiss: I am carrying off nothing of his; let him leave me to go in peace.”
sentences.n: digades = digáis, a subjunctive serving as a polite command, 'tell'. non lo tenga a mal, '(that) he not take it amiss', subjunctive, with que left out; tener a mal, 'to take badly'. de lo so = de lo suyo, 'of what is his'; non … nada, the double negative. lievo = llevo. déxem = déjeme, 'let him let me', subjunctive with me glued on.

sentences.i: The count replied: “That shall not be! For what he did before and what he does now he will pay me in full; the exile shall learn whom he has come to dishonour.”
sentences.n: Respuso = respondió, an old strong preterite. co[m]de, the m Pidal's. esto non será verdad: Pidal's note to v. 979, 'esto no será así', 'this will not be so' (compare vv. 2417 and 3028). Lo de antes e de agora, 'what (was done) before and now'. tódom = todo me: 'all of it to me'. pechar, 'to pay (a fine or tribute)'; lo resumes the object announced at the head of the line. el salido, 'the man gone out', the exile, as in the previous tirada. a quien vino desondrar, 'whom he came to dishonour': vino + bare infinitive.

sentences.t: Tornós el mandadero quanto pudo más.
sentences.l: Turned-himself the messenger as-much he-could more.
sentences.i: The messenger hurried back as fast as he could.
sentences.n: Tornós = tornó + se, 'returned'. mandadero, 'messenger' (mandado, 'message'). quanto pudo más, 'as much as he could', i.e. at full speed.

sentences.t:
Essora lo connosçe mio Çid el de Bivar
que a menos de batalla non pueden den quitar.
sentences.l:
Then it recognizes my Çid he of Bivar
that without battle not they-can from-there free-themselves.
sentences.i: Then my Çid of Vivar sees plainly that short of a battle they cannot get clear of it.
sentences.n: Essora, 'then, at that hour' (esa hora). connosçe, 'recognizes, realizes'; lo anticipates the que-clause. a menos de batalla, 'without a battle'. den = de ende, 'from there, from it'. quitar, here 'to get free, get away' (the subject is the Çid's company, hence pueden).

sentences.t:
“Ya cavalleros, apart fazed la ganançia;
apriessa vos guarnid e metedos en las armas;
sentences.l:
“O knights, apart make the booty;
quickly yourselves arm and put-yourselves in the arms;
sentences.i: “Knights, put the booty to one side; arm yourselves quickly and take up your weapons;
sentences.n: Tirada 57 (assonance á-a) — the Çid's address to his men (Pidal: Arenga del Cid a los suyos). The line-ends are á-a (ganançia, armas, batalla, sobejanas, nada, calças, lanças, vázias, alcança); in ganançia and vázias the final -ia counts as a. Ya cavalleros, 'O knights', the vocative ya. apart fazed: Pidal's note to v. 985, 'apartad', 'set aside', like Latin longe facti sunt, 'they withdrew' (Chronicle of Alfonso VII); fazed = haced, imperative. guarnid, 'arm, equip' (guarnir), with vos before it. metedos = meteos (meted + os): Pidal's note to v. 986, meterse en armas, also at v. 3550, is a synonym of bestir las armas, v. 991.

sentences.t:
el co[m]de don Remont dar nos ha grant batalla,
de moros e de cristianos gentes trae sobejanas,
a menos de batalla non nos dexarié por nada.
sentences.l:
the count don Remont to-give us will great battle,
of Moors and of Christians hosts he-brings excessive,
without battle not us he-would-leave for nothing.
sentences.i: Count Remont is going to give us a great battle; he brings vast hosts of Moors and Christians; short of a battle he would not let us go for anything.
sentences.n: dar nos ha = nos dará, 'he will give us': the split future, infinitive + pronoun + ha. co[m]de, the m Pidal's. sobejanas, 'excessive, very great'. a menos de batalla, 'without a battle', as v. 984. dexarié = dejaría, conditional (old -ié); non … por nada, 'not for anything'.

sentences.t:
Pues adelant irán tras nos, aquí sea la batalla;
apretad los cavallos, e bistades las armas.
sentences.l:
Since forward they-will-go after us, here be the battle;
tighten the horses, and may-you-put-on the arms.
sentences.i: Since they will come on after us wherever we go, let the battle be here: tighten your horses' girths and put on your armour.
sentences.n: Pues, 'since'. adelant … tras nos, 'onward after us', i.e. however far we go. sea, 'let (it) be', subjunctive. apretad los cavallos: Pidal's note to v. 991, before charging one tightens the horse's girth. bistades = vistáis, 'put on', subjunctive used as an exhortation (b for v); bestir las armas, 'to put on one's armour'.

sentences.t:
Ellos vienen cuesta yuso, e todos trahen calças;
elas siellas coçeras e las cinchas amojadas;
sentences.l:
They come slope down, and all bring hose;
and-the saddles light and the girths slack;
sentences.i: They are coming down the slope, and all of them in hose; their saddles light, and their girths slack;
sentences.n: cuesta yuso, 'down the slope' (yuso, 'down', as in ayuso). trahen = traen, 'they wear'. calças, 'hose, leg-coverings' (cloth, without riding-boots: compare v. 994). elas = e las, 'and the' (run together). siellas coçeras: a kind of saddle that Pidal's note to v. 1007 calls insecure, set against the siellas gallegas of v. 994; the precise sense of coçeras is uncertain, and 'light' here is only an approximation. amojadas: probably 'slack, loose', in contrast to the girths the Çid's men are told to tighten (v. 991); Pidal gives no note and the sense is uncertain. The line has no verb: understand 'they have'.

sentences.t:
nos cavalgaremos siellas gallegas, e huesas sobre calças;
çiento cavalleros devemos vençer aquellas mesnadas.
sentences.l:
we will-ride saddles Galician, and boots over hose;
hundred knights we-must defeat those troops.
sentences.i: we shall ride Galician saddles, with boots over our hose: a hundred knights, we are bound to defeat those troops.
sentences.n: cavalgaremos siellas gallegas, 'we will ride Galician saddles', i.e. sit in the heavy saddles of the west, set against the enemy's (Pidal discusses the passage in his introduction, p. 106, to which his note to v. 997 refers). huesas, 'boots' (riding-boots, worn over the hose). çiento cavalleros stands in apposition to the subject 'we'. devemos, 'we must, we are bound to'. mesnadas, 'companies, troops'.

sentences.t:
Antes que ellos lleguen a llaño, presentémosles las lanças
por uno que firgades, tres siellas irán vázias.
sentences.l:
Before that they arrive at plain, let-us-present-them the lances
for one that you-strike, three saddles will-go empty.
sentences.i: Before they reach the level ground, let us meet them with our lances: for every one you strike, three saddles will go empty.
sentences.n: Antes que … lleguen, 'before … they reach' (subjunctive). llaño = llano, 'level ground, the plain'. presentémosles, 'let us present to them', subjunctive of exhortation with les. por uno que firgades, 'for (each) one you strike': firgades = hiráis, subjunctive of ferir. vázias = vacías, 'empty'. Pidal's note to v. 997 refers to v. 1007 and his introduction, p. 106: the enemy's insecure saddles make unhorsing easy.

sentences.t:
Verá Remont Verenguel tras quien vino en alcança
oy en este pinar de Tévar por tollerme la ganançia.”
sentences.l:
Will-see Remont Verenguel after whom he-came in pursuit
today in this pine-wood of Tévar for to-take-from-me the booty.”
sentences.i: Remont Verenguel shall see whom he came chasing today in this pine-wood of Tévar to rob me of my winnings.”
sentences.n: Remont Verenguel, the count's full name (Ramón Berenguer), as printed. tras quien vino en alcança, 'after whom he came in pursuit' (alcança, 'pursuit', from alcançar). oy = hoy. por tollerme, 'in order to take from me': toller, 'to take away', with me glued on.

sentences.t:
Todos son adobados quando mio Çid esto ovo fablado:
las armas avién presas e sedién sobre los cavallos.
sentences.l:
All are equipped when my Çid this had spoken:
the arms they-had taken and they-were-sitting on the horses.
sentences.i: All are ready when my Çid has said this: they had taken up their arms and sat mounted on their horses.
sentences.n: Tirada 58 (assonance á-o) — the Çid wins the battle and the sword Colada (Pidal: El Cid vence la batalla. Gana la espada Colada). The line-ends are á-o (fablado, cavallos, francos, llaño, nasco, grado, enpleando, derrocando, tomado, marcos). adobados, 'equipped, made ready' (adobar). ovo fablado, 'had spoken' (aver + participle, the past anterior). avién presas, 'they had taken', the participle presas agreeing with las armas. sedién, 'they were sitting' (seer, 'to sit'), i.e. mounted.

sentences.i: They saw the host of the Franks coming down the slope; at the foot of the slope, near the level ground, my Çid, he who was born in a good hour, gave the order to charge:
sentences.n: Vi[di]eron = vieron, 'they saw', the old form vidieron, with the di Pidal's. la cuesta yuso, 'down the slope'. fuerça, 'host, army'. los francos: Pidal's note to v. 1002, the Catalans: Catalonia was a march or county of the Carolingian empire, and in memory of that time, even in the twelfth century, Christian and Arab historians commonly call the Catalans 'Franks'. al fondón de, 'at the bottom of'. de’llaño, so printed by Pidal: read as del llaño, 'of the plain', the article's l run into the ll of llaño; çerca es de’llaño, '(it, the host) is near the plain', the moment the Çid wanted (v. 996). mandólos ferir = los mandó ferir, 'ordered them to strike', los the Çid's men. el que en buen ora nasco, the 'born in a good hour' formula (nasco, old preterite of nacer).

sentences.i: His men do it willingly and gladly; pennons and lances, they ply them well, striking down some and unhorsing others.
sentences.n: los sos, 'his (men)'. de voluntad e de grado, 'willingly and gladly'. Los pendones e las lanças … las van enpleando: the object is put first and taken up again by las; ir + gerund for continuing action. pendones, the pennons on the lances. derrocando: Pidal's note to v. 1007, 'derribando', 'throwing down'; remember, he says, that the siellas coçeras of the Catalans were insecure: so the minstrel writes this line instead of the Alexandre's (st. 529) 'a los unos matando, a los otros feriendo'; the Çid's knights did not need to kill their adversaries, nor even wound them, to unhorse them (compare v. 997).

sentences.t:
Vençido a esta batalla el que en buen[a] nasco;
al co[m]de don Remont a preson le a tomado;
sentences.l:
Won-has this battle he who in a-good (hour) was-born;
the count don Remont as prisoner him has taken;
sentences.i: He who was born in a good hour has won this battle; he has taken Count Remont prisoner;
sentences.n: Vençido a = ha vencido, 'has won', the participle put first and a = ha written without h; a esta batalla, the object marked by a. en buen[a] nasco: the noun ora is left out, and Pidal restores the a of buena (in italics) so the adjective agrees with the missing (h)ora: 'born in a good (hour)'. co[m]de, the m Pidal's. a preson, 'as prisoner' (prisión). al co[m]de … le, the object announced and repeated by le. a tomado = ha tomado.

sentences.t: hi gañó a Colada que más vale de mill marcos.
sentences.l: there he-won Colada which more is-worth than thousand marks.
sentences.i: There he won Colada, a sword worth more than a thousand marks.
sentences.n: hi, 'there'. gañó = ganó, 'won'. a Colada: Colada is a sword (Pidal's rubric: Gana la espada Colada), taken from the count, and the a before its name treats it as a person, as with a named horse or sword. más vale de, 'is worth more than'; mill marcos, 'a thousand marks', the mark being a weight of silver (or gold) used in reckoning value.

sentences.i: There he won this battle, by which he did honour to his beard; he took the count and led him off to his tent, and ordered his trusted men to guard him.
sentences.n: Tirada 59 (assonance á-a) — the count of Barcelona a prisoner; he means to let himself die of hunger (Pidal: El conde de Barcelona, prisionero. Quiere dejarse morir de hambre). The line-ends are á-a (barba, levava, mandava, dava, ganancias, adobavan, nada, España, alma, batalla). I, 'there' (hi). por o = por donde, 'whereby'. ondró su barba, 'honoured his beard': the beard is the badge of a man's honour. prísole = le prisó, 'took him' (priso, old preterite of prender), le repeated by al co[m]de, the m Pidal's. tie[nd]a, 'tent', the nd Pidal's. levava = llevaba; mandava, imperfects mixed with preterites. creenderos: Pidal's note to v. 1013, 'servidor fiel', 'faithful servant'; he adds that the poet's details of this capture agree with the second historical capture of the count of Barcelona, in the mountains of Morella in 1090 (his introduction p. 16, and Cantar pp. 865–866). guardar lo mandava = lo mandava guardar.

sentences.i: Out from the tent he sprang; from every side his men were gathering; my Çid was glad, for great are the winnings.
sentences.n: De fuera de la tienda un salto dava, 'from outside the tent he gave a leap': the subject is not named; it is taken here to be the Çid, leaping out of the tent once the count is put under guard, but the line is abrupt and its sense is uncertain (Pidal gives no note). ajunta[van], 'gathered', with the ending van Pidal's. plogo = plugo, 'it pleased' (plazer). ca, 'for'. ganancias, printed here with c (ganançias elsewhere).

sentences.t:
A mio Çid don Rodrigo grant cozínal adobavan;
el conde don Remont non gelo preçia nada;
sentences.l:
For my Çid don Rodrigo great feast-for-him they-were-preparing;
the count don Remont not it-to-him values nothing;
sentences.i: For my Çid don Rodrigo they were preparing a great feast; Count Remont cares nothing for it;
sentences.n: cozínal, so printed: cozina, 'cooked food' (Pidal's note to v. 1017: 'vianda o comida aderezada al fuego', 'food prepared over the fire'), with the pronoun l(e), 'for him', glued on and the accent showing the stress kept on the í; le repeats A mio Çid. A pronoun leaning on a noun rather than a verb is unusual, and the analysis is offered cautiously. adobavan, 'were preparing'. non gelo preçia nada, 'he values it not at all': gelo = se lo, with ge (le) 'to him', most likely the Çid (it is the Çid's feast); the exact force of ge is uncertain. non … nada, double negative.

sentences.t:
adúzenle los comeres, delant gelos paravan,
él non lo quiere comer, a todos los sosañava:
sentences.l:
they-bring-him the dishes, before-him them-to-him they-were-setting,
he not it wants to-eat, at all them he-was-scorning:
sentences.i: They bring him the dishes and set them down before him; he will not eat; he scorned them all:
sentences.n: adúzenle, 'they bring him' (aduzir, 'to bring'). comeres, 'foods, dishes', the infinitive used as a noun. delant gelos paravan, 'they set them before him': gelos = se los, 'them to him'; parar, 'to set, place'. non lo quiere comer, 'he will not eat it'. sosañava, 'scorned, mocked' (sosañar); a todos … los, the object announced and repeated. Present and imperfect alternate freely.

sentences.t:
“Non combré un bocado por quanto ha en toda España,
antes perderé el cuerpo e dexaré el alma,
pues que tales malcalçados me vençieron de batalla.”
sentences.l:
“Not I-will-eat a mouthful for as-much-as there-is in all España,
rather I-will-lose the body and I-will-leave the soul,
since that such ill-shod-ones me defeated in battle.”
sentences.i: “I will not eat a mouthful, not for all there is in Spain; I would rather lose my body and give up my soul, since such ill-shod louts have beaten me in battle.”
sentences.n: combré = comeré, 'I will eat', a syncopated future with a b slipped in (comré > combré). por quanto ha, 'for all there is' (ha = hay). antes, 'rather'. perderé el cuerpo e dexaré el alma, 'I will lose my body and leave my soul', i.e. die. pues que, 'since'. malcalçados, 'badly shod' (mal + calçado), a sneer at the Çid's men; Pidal's note to v. 1023 refers to his introduction, p. 106, and adds that malcalzado was used as a nickname: a sale of 1230 names 'Pedro Martín, grandson of Malcalzado'. de batalla, 'in battle'.
